1.pericope_label: For, behold, in those days, and in that time, when I shall bring again the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem
debates: What time the opening phrase marks
Whether the prophecy can be confined to any past event
Why the promise of restoration is repeated at such length
outliers: Clarke declines to identify the events at all, holding the figures too lofty to be confined to anything before the Christian era and the particular referents at present very uncertain
Wesley keeps two levels at once, making the return under Cyrus a type of a later deliverance that runs through the whole chapter
themes: A jubilee proclaimed, with debts released and prisons opened
A people who were the execration and the dregs of the whole world
Every access to a land closed by the hatred of its neighbours
A year of recompences for a long-running controversy

2.pericope_label: I will also gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and will plead with them there for my people
debates: Which nations are gathered
Whether the valley is a real place or a name for judgment
What indignity the casting of lots describes
outliers: Clarke says there is no such valley in the land at all, so the word must be symbolical, where Ellicott and Calvin both point to a remembered battle whose site supplied the imagery
Calvin rejects the reading that makes the boy given for a harlot a case of prostitution, taking it instead of a price so low that captives were bartered for a meal or a night of pleasure
themes: A valley whose name means the place where the Lord judges
Captives divided by dice among the soldiers who took them
A people sold as the offscourings of mankind at the lowest price
A price spent immediately on gluttony and whoredom

4.pericope_label: Yea, and what have ye to do with me, O Tyre, and Zidon, and all the coasts of Palestine? will ye render me a recompence?
debates: Whose silver and gold is meant
Why the question is asked in the first person
Why the captives were sold so far away
outliers: Ellicott holds the silver and gold to be called Gods because it belonged to his people, not because it was dedicated to the Temple, against Clarke, Wesley and Calvin, who all take it of the sacred vessels
Calvin makes the point of the question that these neighbours were unprovoked volunteers in the war, so that God stands up in his own defence rather than merely his people
themes: Neighbours who took no side until they saw hope of gain
Sacred vessels used to adorn the idols of another nation
Captives shipped beyond the sea so that no road home remained
A people asked whether they can measure strength with God

7.pericope_label: Behold, I will raise them out of the place whither ye have sold them, and will return your recompence upon your own head
debates: When the raising up was fulfilled
How a sale by God differs from the sale it punishes
Which conquests answer to the selling of the enemies sons
outliers: Calvin raises the objection that the people never in fact returned as the words require, rejects the allegorical answer about apostles and martyrs as strained, and settles on a spiritual gathering
Ellicott refers the selling to two kings of an earlier age rather than to the Greek conquerors whom Gill, Clarke and Calvin all name
themes: A restoration that would be as life from the dead
A seller who acts by authority rather than by robbery
Buyers so distant that they were reckoned neighbours to the Indians
Thirty thousand sold out of one city on the day it fell

9.pericope_label: Proclaim ye this among the Gentiles; Prepare war, wake up the mighty men, let all the men of war draw near
debates: Whether the summons to war is serious or ironic
What preparing war literally means
Whether the judgment described is historical or final
outliers: Calvin sets aside the reading that makes the passage an encouragement to the people to brace themselves, holding that it continues the declaration of war upon the nations
Henry reports interpreters who make the whole a picture of the last judgment, and lets it stand beside the historical conquerors he has named
themes: Enemies told to prepare for a war that is already prepared against them
Ploughshares beaten into swords and every peasant made a soldier
War sanctified with religious rites before it is joined
A weak man armed well enough to call himself strong

10.pericope_label: Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruninghooks into spears: let the weak say, I am strong
debates: Whether the valley is a definite place or any place of judgment
Whose the mighty ones are
Whether the harvest is historical or final
outliers: Ellicott takes the mighty ones to be the enemy champions summoned against Jehovah, where Wesley takes them to be the warriors God uses to punish the oppressors of his church
Clarke will not fix the valley to any site, against Gill and Wesley who make it a place in the land that invading armies came up to
themes: A ploughshare hammered back into a sword
Sick men drawn out of their beds and made to bear arms
A land left waste because no one dares go out to it
A press so full that the vats overflow

14.pericope_label: Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision: for the day of the Lord is near in the valley of decision
debates: What the valley of decision is named for
Whether the darkened lights are literal or political
Whether the roar belongs to a temporal deliverance or the last judgment
outliers: Gill argues that no valley actually bearing the name is meant, the place being named from the judgment done in it, which cuts against readings that fix it to a site
Ellicott blends the temporal success of the Jews with the final triumph in the judgment day, where Gill and Clarke read the darkening as the collapse of particular states
themes: A doubled cry over crowds upon crowds filling a valley
A threshing floor where nations are beaten small
Petty princes withdrawing their light from the kingdoms they served
A lion that will not let the prey be taken from him

17.pericope_label: So shall ye know that I am the Lord your God dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain: then shall Jerusalem be holy
debates: What kind of knowledge is promised
Whether the holy city is the restored land or the church
Whether the valley of Shittim is a real place or a symbol
outliers: Clarke argues that Shittim cannot be literally meant because no stream could cross Jordan to reach it, while Wesley keeps it a place in the plains of Moab and makes only the waters spiritual
Calvin cautions that the promised plenty is not meant to occupy the godly with eating and drinking, against readings that take the material prosperity for the substance of the promise
themes: A knowledge held by faith and a knowledge held by enjoyment
A city no alien may so much as pass through
Mountains trickling with new wine and hills running with milk
A dry acacia plain reached by water from the temple

19.pericope_label: Egypt shall be a desolation, and Edom shall be a desolate wilderness, for the violence against the children of Judah
debates: Whether Egypt and Edom are named as nations or as types
In whose land the innocent blood was shed
Whether the closing cleansing is vengeance on the enemies or pardon for the people
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch place the bloodshed in the offenders own territory and date it from the slaying of the Hebrew boys and Edom throwing off the dominion of Judah, where Calvin prefers to place it in Judea itself and calls the pollution of consecrated land the more atrocious crime
Clarke follows the rendering that makes the closing promise an act of vengeance not yet executed, where Ellicott, Gill and Wesley take it for pardon extended to the hitherto unpardoned
themes: Two old enemies left as dry wilderness while the hills run with milk
Blood shed by nations that had been asked for refuge
A land inhabited from generation to generation
Pollution left so long that it has gone putrid
